clue.text: In the martyred village a little boy (odd boy) used to wear it …

definitions.note: a clause, not a noun: the answer is the thing a little boy used to wear

indicators.note: odd means peculiar or out of true, so the second boy is set out in a strange order
the boys' names sit inside the name of the village, so the village wraps around them

parts.note: Lidice, the Czech village destroyed by the Nazis in 1942
Bert is a short form of Albert or Herbert
the word boy with its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A boy in a tragic Czech village once wore some garment, the sentence trailing off into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into 10: this was a warm vest children wore under a shirt. The village is split open so the two boys can sit in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A liberty bodice was a sleeveless cotton undergarment that British children wore through much of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Up in arms at taunt in pub at social worker

indicators.note: one word goes inside the other, so the pub holds the taunt

parts.note: an inn is a pub
a dig is a jibe
ants are social insects, and many are workers

explanation.surface: Someone is furious at being mocked in the pub by a social worker.
explanation.walkthrough: IN(DIG)N plus ANT. A 'social worker' here is an insect, not a caseworker.
explanation.definitionFit: To be up in arms is an idiom for being angrily outraged, which is what an indignant person feels.

clue.text: Bird that won't start to apologise

indicators.note: a word that will not start loses its opening letter

parts.note: to regret is to express sorrow or apologise, as in 'regrets he cannot attend'

explanation.surface: A bird stubbornly refuses to begin saying sorry.
explanation.definitionFit: An egret is a white heron, a wading bird of marshes and shallow water.

clue.text: Time and money, that's what's wrong

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
the rouble is the Russian currency

explanation.surface: A complaint that lack of time and cash is the root of every problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking 'what's the trouble?' means asking what is wrong, so the noun names the problem or fault.

clue.text: 7 on sand's keeping 7 in fripperies

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the sands hold the second star's surname within them

parts.note: 7 down is CLARA, and Clara Butt was a celebrated English contralto
taken as written
read as the plural, sands
Clara Bow was the 1920s Hollywood 'It' girl

explanation.surface: A woman lounging on a beach dressed in frilly finery.
explanation.walkthrough: Each 7 stands for a different Clara, so the solver needs her surname, not CLARA itself. The second Clara goes in just before the last S of the sands.
explanation.definitionFit: Buttons and bows are trivial decorative trimmings, and the phrase is the title of a 1948 song about such frills.

clue.text: Terminate — put a full stop — to poem on bad hat

indicators.note: something bad is spoilt or out of order, so the hat's letters go astray

parts.note: a full stop is a dot
an ode is a lyric poem
the letters of hat mixed up

explanation.surface: A writer is told to finish off a poem about an ugly hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'put a full stop' look like a gloss on 'Terminate'; it is wordplay, and 'put' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone to death is an idiom for killing them; figuratively, to overuse something until it is finished.

clue.text: Miss Butt and Miss Bow see century by batsman

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
Brian Lara, the West Indies batsman

explanation.surface: Two ladies are invited to watch a batsman score a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: Clara Butt was a contralto and Clara Bow a silent-film star; the shared first name is what the two Misses have in common.
explanation.definitionFit: Both women were called Clara: the singer Dame Clara Butt and the actress Clara Bow, so their shared forename fits.

clue.text: "Miss Buss and Miss Beale ________ " need a friend to stop cuddles

definitions.note: a fill-in-the-blank: the answer is the missing line of the rhyme

indicators.note: to need is to require work, so the following words must be reworked into new order

parts.note: all twenty letters of these four words taken as fodder

explanation.surface: Two prim headmistresses, untouched by love, would need a friend to stop all the cuddling.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme mocked Frances Buss and Dorothea Beale, Victorian pioneers of girls' schools: 'Miss Buss and Miss Beale / Cupid's darts do not feel'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing words complete the well-known Victorian rhyme about two unmarried headmistresses immune to romance.

clue.text: Mrs Buck and Mrs Bailey make 22

parts.note: surface reading: two married women, perhaps neighbours
setter's reading: Pearl Buck the novelist and Pearl Bailey the singer, each a Mrs and each a Pearl, so mothers called Pearl

explanation.surface: Two housewives get together to produce something.
explanation.walkthrough: Like 7 and 8, the clue pairs two famous women sharing a first name; here 'Mrs' plays the part of mother, and the shared name is Pearl.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre, the answer to 22, is the iridescent lining of mollusc shells, commonly known by this name.

clue.text: … with a shirt, perhaps, to be glossed over

definitions.meaning: continuing 1: the bodice was worn with a shirt, under a coat
a coat of paint applied first, then covered by gloss

explanation.surface: A child's vest, worn with a shirt, is something better not mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: Read on from 1: the garment was worn with a shirt beneath the outer clothes, which splits as UNDER COAT. 'Glossed over' sounds like ignored, but means painted.
explanation.definitionFit: An undercoat is the primer layer of paint, later covered by a gloss topcoat; read as two words it is clothing worn beneath a coat.

clue.text: President, a change from Botha

indicators.note: a change from a word is that word altered, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: P.W. Botha, the apartheid-era South African leader, taken as letters

explanation.surface: A new South African president marks a break from the apartheid regime.
explanation.walkthrough: Thabo Mbeki became South Africa's president in 1999, and his first name rearranges the surname of the old apartheid leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Thabo Mbeki was President of South Africa from 1999 to 2008, succeeding Nelson Mandela.

clue.text: Entered a mass with some value

wordplay.note: got in, written with its two words in the other order

explanation.surface: Someone joined a church service and paid their dues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entered' becomes 'got in', and the two little words are then written in the other order. 'Mass' is a lump, not a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingot is a cast block of precious metal such as gold, a lump of material worth money.

clue.text: Man about town, or rather Georgian city, in a massacre

parts.note: a blood is an old word for a fashionable young man about town
Bath, the English spa city famed for its Georgian terraces

explanation.surface: A dandy, or rather a whole city, caught up in a slaughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Georgian' points to the 18th-century architecture of Bath in Somerset, not the country of Georgia or the US state.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloodbath is a scene of wholesale slaughter, making it a vivid synonym for a massacre.

clue.text: Decoration to cover broken leg

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, so the limb's letters are put back in a new order

parts.note: to span is to stretch across or cover
leg jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone dresses a fracture in something festive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' looks like a container signal wrapping the leg, but it simply supplies the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A spangle is a small glittering sequin sewn onto clothing as ornament.

clue.text: A sportsman is a fool, keeping up old run

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the fool wraps around what follows

parts.note: a goose is a silly person

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written before being turned
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A sports commentator dismisses a player as an idiot who keeps an ancient record going.
explanation.definitionFit: A good loser accepts defeat gracefully, which describes a sporting competitor with fine manners.

clue.text: Unfairly denigrate south German regions

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south
the Länder are the federal states of Germany

explanation.surface: A complaint that southern German states are being unjustly maligned.
explanation.definitionFit: To slander is to make false, damaging spoken statements about a person, unjustly blackening their name.

clue.text: They are expected at length at scene of combat

definitions.text: They are expected at length at scene of combat

parts.note: due means expected, as a train is due
L is the abbreviation for length
the lists were the fenced ground where knights jousted

explanation.surface: Combatants are awaited, perhaps at a sword's length, on the field of honour.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole sentence defines the answer while also building it: fighters are expected at the lists, where they meet at arm's length.
explanation.definitionFit: Duellists are people fighting a formal single combat, who naturally turn up at the appointed field of battle.

clue.text: Instrument that's low even if fleet

parts.note: even if means although, and its low or informal spelling is altho
RN is the Royal Navy, Britain's fleet

explanation.surface: An instrument with a deep voice, however nimble it may be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' suggests a deep note, apt for a horn, but it marks the slangy spelling of the conjunction.
explanation.definitionFit: The althorn is a valved brass instrument of the saxhorn family, pitched in the alto range.

clue.text: See 8
50 in a bundle with keys

definitions.note: a prepositional phrase: it describes the ash tree the leaf comes from

indicators.note: the number sits inside the bundle, which wraps around it

parts.note: a sheaf is a bundle, as of corn or papers
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Fifty items tied in a bundle along with a set of keys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keys' are not for locks: ash trees bear winged seeds called keys, so the answer is a leaf of that tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash trees produce clusters of winged seeds known as keys, so an ash leaf comes from a tree bearing them.

clue.text: See 5
A record comes back in, coloured to prevent corrosion

definitions.note: a purpose phrase: tinplated describes metal coated for this purpose

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the coloured word

parts.note: tinted means lightly coloured
taken as written

indicators.note: coming back means returning, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: An old vinyl record returns to the shop, painted to stop it rusting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coloured' sits next to the definition and looks like part of it, but it is the wrapper.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinplated iron or steel has a thin tin coating precisely to stop it rusting.

clue.text: Pole (a measure of land) produced by molluscs

parts.note: N is the North Pole
an acre is a unit of land area

explanation.surface: A pole, the old land measure, turns out to be made by shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: A pole is also an old measure of length, so the bracket seems to explain it; it is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre is the pearly substance secreted by oysters and other shellfish to line their shells.

clue.text: Temporary increase in acceleration among blue characters

indicators.note: characters are odd letters to be set out anew, so the word is reshuffled
something among others sits in their midst

parts.note: the letters of blue reordered
g is the symbol for acceleration due to gravity

explanation.surface: A sudden spurt of speed among some foul-mouthed people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue characters' reads as rude people; it is the letters of blue rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulge is a temporary rise in numbers, as in the post-war baby bulge.

clue.text: Degree for Tory writer and painter

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree
Con is short for Conservative

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician is awarded an honorary degree for creative work.
explanation.walkthrough: Two different men share the name: Francis Bacon the Elizabethan essayist and Francis Bacon the 20th-century painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the philosopher-essayist Francis Bacon and the expressionist artist Francis Bacon bear this surname.

clue.text: Avoids affectionate address

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dodges, as in lowering the head
second meaning: a fond way of addressing someone, common in northern England

explanation.walkthrough: 'Address' is a form of words used to speak to someone, not a location.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck is to dodge or evade, and 'ducks' is a warm British term of endearment like 'love'.

clue.text: Spell-breaker's recipe: get gold in tax first

indicators.note: one piece placed inside the tax word

parts.note: excise is a duty on goods
or is gold in heraldry
R is the abbreviation for recipe, as on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A witch's formula for undoing a spell: put gold in before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' says the gold goes into the tax before the recipe letter is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An exorciser drives out demons or evil spirits, breaking the hold of an enchantment or curse.

clue.text: Canines would be located on the Riviera by such cruelty

parts.words: Canines would be located on the Riviera
parts.note: surface reading: dogs would be found on the French coast

parts.words: Canines would be located on the Riviera
parts.note: setter's reading: remove the central letter of canines and you have Cannes, a Riviera resort

explanation.surface: Dogs dumped on the Côte d'Azur by heartless owners.
explanation.walkthrough: Canines has seven letters; take away its heart, the middle I, and Cannes is left. So the state of being without a heart puts canines on the Riviera.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartlessness means a lack of compassion or pity, which is the essence of cruelty.
